name: Hanoi
info: Hanoi is a city on the Red River in northern Vietnam, established as the capital Thăng Long by the Lý dynasty in 1010, later the capital of French Indochina and of North Vietnam, and now the capital of Vietnam.

facts.founded: In 1010 the first Lý emperor, Lý Thái Tổ, moved the capital of Đại Việt to the site of the Đại La Citadel and named the city Thăng Long; a fortified settlement had stood at the centre of what later became Hanoi since the middle of the fifth century CE.
facts.where: On the Red River in northern Vietnam, in a region of monsoon-influenced humid subtropical climate with four seasons.
facts.known: Thăng Long, capital of Đại Việt from 1010; the Temple of Literature; the Old Quarter and its 36 streets; the capital of French Indochina from 1902; the capital of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam; the capital of unified Vietnam from 1976
facts.today: Hanoi is the capital of Vietnam and its second most populous centrally governed city.

t: A fortified settlement stood at the centre of what later became Hanoi from the middle of the fifth century CE, under the names Tống Bình, Đại La and later Thăng Long, and Lý Thái Tổ made it the capital of Đại Việt in 1010.
The city kept its status under the Lý and the Lê, lost it to Huế in 1802, was renamed Hà Nội in 1831, and became the capital of French Indochina in 1902.
It was the capital of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam from 1945 and of North Vietnam from 1954, and in 1976 it became the capital of the unified Socialist Republic of Vietnam.
dyk: Lý Thái Tổ named his new capital Thăng Long, 'ascending dragon', after claiming to have seen a dragon ascending the Red River, and Hanoi's older names such as Long Biên and Long Đỗ also featured the dragon.
ev: A fortified citadel, later named Cổ Loa, is built in what later became Hanoi

sections.origins:
Hanoi stands on the Red River in northern Vietnam. Archaeologists working in Ba Vì and Đông Anh in 1971 and 1972 found pebbles with traces of carving that are relics of the Sơn Vi culture, dating from 10,000 to 20,000 years ago, and a study in 1998 and 1999 north of Đồng Mô Lake in Sơn Tây found Sơn Vi relics of about 20,000 years ago. Geological data show that during the Holocene transgression the sea rose and immersed low-lying areas, so that from about 10,000 to about 4,000 years ago Hanoi in general was completely underwater. It is believed that the region has been continuously inhabited for the last 4,000 years.

In around the third century BCE a fortified citadel, later named Cổ Loa, was built in what later became Hanoi. It was the first political centre of the Vietnamese civilisation of the pre-Sinitic era, and its outer embankment covered 600 hectares. In 179 BCE Nanyue annexed the area, and Zhao Tuo left the indigenous chiefs in control of the population; for the first time the region formed part of a polity headed by a Chinese ruler. By the middle of the fifth century CE the Chinese Liu Song dynasty had founded a fortified settlement at the centre of what later was Hanoi, as the seat of a new district called Tống Bình (Songping) within Giao Chỉ commandery. The name refers to the pacification of the area by the dynasty.
sections.growth:
The Tang governor Zhang Boyi rebuilt the citadel of Songping around 767 as La Thành, after he defeated a Javanese raid, and it was expanded in the first half of the ninth century. After Gao Pian recaptured the city in 866 he built a wall around it measuring 6,344 metres, with some sections more than eight metres high. Đại La then had approximately 25,000 residents, among them Persian, Arab, Indian, Cham and Javanese communities and Nestorian Christians. Medieval Muslim sources between the 9th and 12th centuries called the city Luqin.

In 1010 Lý Thái Tổ made the site the capital of Đại Việt as Thăng Long. The Temple of Literature, site of the oldest university in Vietnam, was started in 1010, and the One Pillar Pagoda was built in 1049, based on a dream of King Lý Thái Tông. In the 17th century, when the city was called Đông Kinh, Western diplomats estimated its population at about 100,000. The Old Quarter near Hoàn Kiếm Lake kept its street layout: at the beginning of the 20th century Hanoi consisted of the 36 streets, the citadel and some newer French buildings south of the lake, and each street had merchants and households specialising in a trade such as silk, jewellery or bamboo.

After the French took control in 1888 they built boulevards, villas and government buildings. Paul Doumer, governor-general from 1898 to 1902, played a role in the city's planning, and Ernest Hébrard designed a master plan in 1924 that was partially implemented.
sections.rulers:
Han rule followed the Han conquest of Nanyue in 111 BCE. The Liu Song seat of Tống Bình was the capital of Annam under the Tang from 679, and Chinese control in northern Vietnam ended de facto in 880, when the Tang army in Annam mutinied and took Đại La. In 1010 Lý Thái Tổ, the first ruler of the Lý dynasty, moved the capital of Đại Việt there. Thăng Long remained the capital until 1397, when the capital moved to Thanh Hóa, and the city became Đông Đô, the Eastern Capital.

The Ming dynasty invaded and occupied Đại Việt in 1408 and renamed the city Dongguan. In 1428 the Lam Sơn uprising under Lê Lợi overthrew Chinese rule, and he founded the Lê dynasty and renamed the city Đông Kinh, the source of the Western name Tonkin. When the Nguyễn dynasty was established in 1802, Gia Long moved the capital to Huế. In 1831 Minh Mạng renamed the city Hà Nội. The French military occupied Hanoi in 1873 and it passed to them ten years later; it was in the protectorate of Tonkin and became the capital of French Indochina in 1902.

Japan occupied French Indochina in September 1940, and on 2 September 1945 Hồ Chí Minh proclaimed the independence of Vietnam, with Hanoi as the capital of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. The French reoccupied the city in February 1947. From 1949 to 1954 Hanoi was under the State of Vietnam, and in 1954 it became the capital of North Vietnam. In 1976 it became the capital of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam.
sections.life:
The city's names record its changing peoples and rulers. Several of the older ones, such as Long Biên and Long Đỗ, feature the dragon, linked to the curved formation of the Red River around the city. Under the Tang, Đại La had Persian, Arab, Indian, Cham and Javanese communities and Nestorian Christians, and Muslim traders knew the city as Luqin.

In the Old Quarter commerce started hundreds of years ago and consisted mostly of family businesses. The street names reflected the trades, and some streets remained exclusively in their original commerce. Over six decades of French colonisation and centuries of cultural influence from China shaped the designs of the old houses: the fronts of some combine French-style columns, Confucian scrolls, the Taoist yin-yang sign and the Buddhist lotus. The French colonial style became dominant elsewhere, in tree-lined boulevards such as Phan Đình Phùng, Hoàng Diệu and Trần Phú and in villas, mansions and government buildings, and some colonial structures mixed French and Vietnamese styles.

During the colonial period Hanoi, as the capital of French Indochina, attracted French, Chinese and Vietnamese people from the surrounding areas. The population was 132,145 in the 1940s. In the 2019 census the Viet (Kinh) accounted for 98.66 per cent of the population, followed by the Mường at 0.77 per cent and the Tày at 0.24 per cent, and more than 50 ethnic groups lived in the city.
sections.crises:
In March 40 CE Trưng Trắc and Trưng Nhị, daughters of an aristocratic Lạc family of the Mê Linh district, led a rebellion against the Han that gained the support of about 65 towns and settlements. In 42 the Han emperor sent the general Ma Yuan with 32,000 men to suppress it. The rebellion was defeated the next year, and Ma Yuan captured and decapitated the two sisters and sent their heads to the Han court at Luoyang.

In 863 Nanzhao and local rebels besieged Jincheng and overran the Tang garrisons, and in 866 Gao Pian recaptured the city and drove them out. The Ming invasion and occupation of Đại Việt began in 1408 and lasted until the uprising of Lê Lợi in 1428.

The Japanese occupation of French Indochina began in September 1940, and in March 1945 Japan overthrew French rule in Hanoi. After the French returned in February 1947, eight years of fighting between French and Democratic Republic forces followed, and the People's Army of Vietnam and the International Control Commission occupied the city on 10 October 1954 under the 1954 Geneva Conference. The city had 53 thousand inhabitants in 1954. During the Vietnam War, from 1955 to 1975, North Vietnam, Hanoi included, was attacked by United States and South Vietnamese air forces.
sections.legacy:
The Temple of Literature, the One Pillar Pagoda and the Flag Tower of Hanoi are among the sites that survive from the imperial period, and in 2004 part of the 900-year-old Hanoi Citadel was discovered in central Hanoi, near Ba Đình Square. The Old Quarter keeps most of its original street layout, and the French colonial buildings include the National Museum of Vietnamese History, the Vietnam National Museum of Fine Arts and the old Indochina Medical College.

Hanoi's area changed several times. By 1961 it covered 584 square kilometres and had a population of 91,000, and in 1978 the National Assembly enlarged it to 2,136 square kilometres with a population of 2.5 million. On 1 August 2008 Hà Tây Province, Mê Linh District and four communes of Lương Sơn District were merged into it, bringing the population to about 6.2 million. After public protest against the redevelopment of culturally significant areas the national government introduced a low-rise policy around Hoàn Kiếm Lake, and Ba Đình District is also protected from commercial redevelopment.

Hanoi is today the capital of Vietnam and its second most populous centrally governed city, with about 8.7 million people. It hosts the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long, the Hồ Chí Minh Mausoleum, Hoàn Kiếm Lake and West Lake.

summary: Hanoi, on the Red River in northern Vietnam, grew from a fortified settlement of the fifth century CE into Thăng Long, the capital of Đại Việt from 1010. It was the capital of French Indochina and of North Vietnam, and since 1976 it has been the capital of Vietnam.
references: Georges Boudarel, Hanoi: City Of The Rising Dragon (Rowman & Littlefield Publishers, Inc., 2002)
Quoc Vuong Tran, Hanoi: From the Origins to the 19th Century (Xunhasaba, 1977)
William S. Logan, Hanoi: Biography of a City (University of Washington Press, 2000)
Michael G. Vann, The Great Hanoi Rat Hunt: Empire, Disease, and Modernity in French Colonial Vietnam (Oxford University Press, 2018)
notes: Only wp/hanoi.txt exists; there is no hanoi-history article, so the city's own article alone was used.

START: the article gives no single founding date for Hanoi. I used 1010 (Thăng Long established by Lý Thái Tổ) with circa false; the article also dates a fortified settlement (Tống Bình) to the middle of the fifth century CE and Cổ Loa to around the third century BCE, both described as 'what later became Hanoi'. The editor may prefer c. 450 CE as start.

The article says the city was first called Long Biên, Tống Bình and Long Đỗ 'sometime in 450' and elsewhere gives the Liu Song commandery as between AD 454 and 464; I wrote only 'by the middle of the fifth century'.
The article says the Tang renamed the region Annam in 679 with Songping as capital; I kept this.

The article gives the population in 2026 as 8.7 million; written as 'about 8.7 million' without the year. The 2008 merger figure appears as 6,232,940 and 6.233 million; I wrote 'about 6.2 million'. The 1954 and 1961 figures (53 thousand and 91,000) are as given and look inconsistent with the 1940s figure of 132,145 and the 1999 figure of 2,672,122; I used the 1954 figure only, but the editor should check it.
The 1954 'occupied the city on 10 October' is worded as the article words it (People's Army of Vietnam of the DRV and the International Control Commission); worded as the article words it.
The Temple of Literature 'site of the oldest university in Vietnam which was started in 1010': the article's wording, kept as the article's claim.
Left out: environment, climate, economy, development plans, civil society, tourism, education, transport, sports, twin cities, UNESCO title (present-day or ranking material).

The article's prose is garbled in places ('Hanoi was conquered ... passed to them ten years later', 'since 1888 the city had been a French concession'); I used the 1873 occupation, the 1883 cession wording and the 1888 French control as given.
The Nguyễn change of the city's characters in 1802 (to 昇隆) was left out for space.
